cases.title: Bumbuna hydroelectric dam: 41 households resettled, two villages left out of compensation
cases.place: Bumbuna, Kalanthuba chiefdom, Tonkolili District, Sierra Leone
cases.point: Bumbuna town, below the dam on the Seli River (OpenStreetMap). The Bank's documents give no coordinates for the 38 villages that lost land to the reservoir.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Grants IDA-H1700 and IDA-H6250 for the Bumbuna Hydroelectric Environmental and Social Management Project (P086801). An IDA grant of US$12.5 million was approved on 16 June 2005 alongside a partial risk guarantee for the dam; the grant was later raised to US$22.0 million. The original commitment of SDR 8.30 million became SDR 13.21 million disbursed. Effectiveness was 19 December 2006 against an original date of 26 October 2005, and closing was 30 June 2013 against an original date of 31 August 2009. The project was restructured seven times and renamed in 2011, when the guarantee was cancelled and US$9.5 million moved into the environmental and social work. Outcomes were rated Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 July 2014).

lenders.name: African Development Bank
lenders.role: US$3.8 million in the project's original and revised financing plan. Italy (US$19.9 million), OPEC (US$8.4 million) and the Netherlands (US$0.3 million) were in the original plan and nil in the revised plan (World Bank completion report, Annex 1).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, safety of dams, natural habitats, forests and cultural property. An exception to the Bank's resettlement policy was granted so that IDA grant money could pay 'legacy' compensation for property and farmland lost when the transmission line foundations were first built in the 1990s. A special account was set up for transmission line compensation, to be used once a legal framework existed.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the resettlement plan for the dam and reservoir area was updated in 2008 and implemented before the first phase of impoundment, and that by December 2008 it had completed 'resettlement and compensation covering 38 villages, 599 households, and 5,033 PAPs', emergency food aid over two years, 'land for land exchange for 41 households (186 people) in five villages covering 179.3 hectares of agricultural lands', and cash compensation to 171 farmers with 117 hectares of partly or fully flooded farmland. The resettlement completion report records that 41 houses in five villages were resettled for US$286,370, with a further US$1.4 million in allowances across 38 villages for lost economic trees, opening new land, moving costs, cultural land and sacred sites. For the 161 kV transmission line, the 2005 plan found 367 households inside the right of way; under revised rules in 2009 roughly 910 households and 1,565 affected people were found within the built-up parts of the right of way, and about 70 to 80 per cent of them chose to move elsewhere. A new shoreline survey in 2011 found roughly 100 new affected people, that 142 of the 507 or so boundary markers placed in 2007 had gone missing after impoundment, and that the land was generally cultivated by more than 500 'shoreline farmers' using it in the dry season. A 2024 master's thesis in sociology at Colorado State University by Katherine Stevick reports a different picture for two villages the Bank's documents do not name. Stevick's own interviews and participatory mapping in Kalanthuba chiefdom in 2023 found that neither Kadala nor Kamathor received financial compensation for the land they lost. She writes that reports held at the project camp describe how compensation was paid to affected villages in Kalanthuba, 'with Kadal and Kamathor mistakenly omitted'; that the Bank's maps were wrong and Kadala, projected to lose a sacred site but no farmland, lost most of its farmland; and that Kadala received gifts and development assistance instead of payment. She records Kadala as a village of about 15 households and Kamathor as holding between 250 and 350 people. Her figures for land lost to the project are more than 50 per cent of historic holdings for Kamathor and 100 per cent for Kadala; she also records that most of the land Kamathor lost had already been taken earlier, for the dam construction site, the contractor's camp and surrounding buildings, work that began in the mid-1970s.
cases.ecosystem: The reservoir and a buffer zone took land for the Bumbuna Conservation Area, chartered by Sierra Leone's parliament in 2008 and covering 3,532 hectares entirely inside Kalanthuba chiefdom, created after the Bank's environmental study showed the dam would harm a rare population of West African chimpanzees. A larger offset was later added by upgrading the Loma Mountains forest reserve to a national park. Stevick's 2024 thesis reports that she found no record of any process to compensate for land taken for the conservation area, and that staff of the Bumbuna Watershed Management Authority knew of none.
cases.killed_note: Two boys from Bumbuna Town died in January 2009 during one of the large water releases from the dam. The World Bank's completion report calls it an accidental death and says it prompted more clearly defined emergency warning procedures.
cases.displaced_label: people in 41 households physically moved and given replacement land (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8,862 for this project. The World Bank's completion report says resettlement and compensation covered 38 villages, 599 households and 5,033 project-affected persons by December 2008, and that 41 households, 186 people, in five villages were physically moved and given replacement land. Those 5,033 are people compensated or covered by the plan, not people moved. For the transmission line the report gives roughly 910 households and 1,565 affected people inside the built-up right of way in 2009, with 70 to 80 per cent of them choosing to move elsewhere, and gives no count of how many did. The documents do not explain the difference from ICIJ's figure, and no document found gives a single total of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The Bank says the three resettlement targets were fully met and that livelihoods were restored to pre-project levels 'barring a few cases where the PAPs are not contactable'. The same report says compensation remained to be paid on legacy claims and that 95 people could not be located because they had migrated out of the area, and that at closing in June 2013 'conformance to the provisions of the Bank's environmental and social safeguards policies was incomplete', with payment of compensation to the few remaining affected people among the items the Bank would keep supervising after the project ended. The Independent Evaluation Group's review posted on 2 December 2015 records the same unfinished items and says the completion report discusses only the environmental and resettlement aspects, with 'little or no information' on the other four safeguard policies the project triggered. The borrower and implementing agencies did not comment on the completion report despite multiple reminders. Stevick's thesis reports that electricity reached Bumbuna Town and Kamankay village in 2014 after local protests and a direct appeal to the president, that it is expensive and reaches only a handful of wealthier households, and that there is almost no electricity in Kamathor and none in the chiefdom's other 42 villages.

cases.confidence_note: The compensation and resettlement figures are the World Bank's own, in its completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, so on those the lender is reporting on its own project. The finding that Kadala and Kamathor were left out of compensation is from one independent source, a 2024 master's thesis in sociology at Colorado State University based on the researcher's own interviews and participatory mapping in 2023; it is her field research rather than an established record, and the Bank's documents do not mention either village. Her figures for land loss cover everything the two villages lost to the scheme from the mid-1970s onwards, not only what was taken under this grant. This map carries a separate case at the same place, 'Tonkolili Iron Ore and the Bumbuna Shootings', which concerns African Minerals' iron ore operation and a police shooting in Bumbuna town in April 2012. That is a different operation with a different financier, and the two are not one episode.

lvwhy.project: An IDA grant financed the environmental and social management of the dam, including the resettlement plans for the reservoir and the transmission line.
lvwhy.land: Farmland and houses were taken for the reservoir, a buffer zone, a conservation area and the transmission line right of way, and 41 households were moved to replacement land.

cases.title: Kibera and Mukuru railway relocation: 1,256 households moved, the rest left waiting
cases.place: Kibera and Mukuru settlements along the Kenya-Uganda railway, Nairobi, Kenya
cases.point: Kibera, Nairobi (OpenStreetMap), at one of the two three-kilometre safety zones. The second is in Mukuru, about 11 km east.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-4147 (SDR 18.2 million, US$25.6 million), IDA-4148 (SDR 83.03 million, US$117.3 million), IDA-4149 (SDR 25.5 million, US$35.9 million), grant IDA-H2020 (SDR 10.4 million, US$14.6 million) and additional credit IDA-4977 (SDR 18.6 million, US$26.2 million) for the East Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project (P079734), covering Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania. Approved 24 January 2006, effective 5 June 2006, closing extended from 30 September 2011 to 30 September 2015. Additional financing of US$30 million was approved in June 2011 for the enlarged relocation plan, and the project's safeguards category was changed from B to A at the same time. Actual IDA financing was US$225.51 million. The line item for implementing the relocation action plan rose from US$11.00 million at appraisal to US$92.80 million actual, of which IDA paid US$39.10 million and the government of Kenya US$53.70 million. Outcome was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 September 2016; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, 9 May 2017).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA partial risk guarantees)
lenders.role: Guarantee IDA-B0090 of up to US$45 million for the Kenyan subsidiary and IDA-B0100 of up to US$15 million for the Ugandan subsidiary of Rift Valley Railways Holdings Limited, the concessionaire of the Kenya-Uganda railway (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project funded a relocation action plan to clear a safety zone along the railway through two informal settlements. The Bank wanted the cleared strip kept to 10.4 metres, 5.2 metres each side of the tracks; the government of Kenya wanted 60 metres. After a train derailment in Kibera in 2009 the government returned to the wider figure, and a new plan in January 2011 set a right of way of 40 metres with resettlement of households in the next 10 metres on each side, a total work area of 60 metres in two three-kilometre safety zones, one in Kibera and one in Mukuru, with a nine-metre wall between the settlements and the tracks. A Resettlement Management Unit was set up in 2011. When it became clear the plan could not be finished by closing, the government agreed to put about US$860,000 from the remaining credit into an escrow account for owners of multiple plots.

companies.name: Rift Valley Railways Holdings Limited
companies.role: Concessionaire of the Kenya-Uganda railway, whose Kenyan and Ugandan subsidiaries held the IDA partial risk guarantees
companies.desc: Holding company of the 25-year concession to run the Kenya-Uganda railway. The World Bank's completion report records the weak performance of the concession as a serious shortfall of the project's early years.

cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the expropriation was originally estimated at 3,400 structures or households, 'involving possibly 10,000 people', in settlements it puts at about 250,000 residents for Mukuru and about 1 million for Kibera, and that after the 2011 plan 'the number of households requiring resettlement grew from 3,400 to about 10,000, involving some 30,000 people'. By the end of January 2016, 51 per cent of the needed residential units and 29 per cent of the needed business units had been built and 1,256 households had been relocated. By September 2016 a social audit had cut the requirement from 9,005 units to 7,429, and the report says 3,214 affected people had been relocated, 324 pupils had moved from informal schools to ten public schools, and 70 grievance cases were pending before the Grievance Appeals Board. The Independent Evaluation Group reads the 1,256 households as involving those 3,214 people and puts them at just over 13 per cent and 10 per cent of the estimated totals, and says the relocation programme was only 30 per cent complete at closing and still going on in January 2017. Amnesty International, in urgent action 80/10 with the issue date 15 April 2010, recorded that Kenya Railways had placed notices in newspapers on 21 March telling people living and working in shacks by the lines that they would be prosecuted unless they tore down their shacks and left within 30 days, and that more than 50,000 people, most of them living alongside the railway lines in Nairobi, faced forced eviction with no alternative housing or resettlement offered. It noted that a Relocation Action Plan for Improving Safety along the Kenya Railway Line, commissioned in response to similar planned evictions in 2005 and published the following year, had never been implemented.
cases.killed_note: A train derailment in Kibera in 2009 caused several fatalities, according to the Bank's completion report, which gives no number. Those deaths are not counted here: the derailment was a railway accident, not an act of the project, and the report ties it to the project only in that it let the government press for a wider cleared strip.
cases.displaced_label: households relocated by the end of January 2016 (World Bank completion report; Independent Evaluation Group)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11,722 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 1,256 households relocated by the end of January 2016 and 3,214 project-affected persons relocated by September 2016, and says the plan after 2011 covered about 10,000 households and some 30,000 people. The Independent Evaluation Group calls the relocated numbers just over 13 per cent and 10 per cent of the estimated totals and the programme 30 per cent complete at closing. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Independent Evaluation Group rated the project's outcome moderately unsatisfactory and said the relocation plan, revised in 2011, only started in late 2013 and was incomplete at closing. The Bank's own lesson from the project is that it treated the clearance 'as a standard linear resettlement typically associated with a road or rail investment', that this is hard to apply in settlements like Kibera and Mukuru, that the government 'clearly wanted to clear the whole reserve', and that the work 'goes well beyond compliance with OP 4.12'. Residents of Soweto, Laini Saba and Mashimoni who gave up their homes for promised flats at Ng'ando in Jamhuri Estate told the Daily Nation they were still in temporary structures with no latrines or running water. The article says 560 families, through their chairperson Peter Kinyua, petitioned Parliament to make Kenya Railways resettle them; that the plan had called for 9,005 units between 2013 and 2015; that of more than 600 units in their scheme about 100 were complete except for the sewer line, about 300 were unfinished and deteriorating and about 200 had not been started; and that residents had been told the work would take eight months and it had taken about eight years. It reports that Kenya Railways insists it has not received government funds to finish the work, and that residents said it still sent reminders to pay rent for the unfinished units.

cases.title: Kawanda-Masaka power line: armed police used to string a line over unpaid land
cases.place: Kawanda-Masaka 220 kV transmission line corridor, from Wakiso to Masaka, Uganda
cases.point: Masaka city (OpenStreetMap), at the southern end of the 137 km line. The residents who spoke to the Daily Monitor were in Nyendo-Ssenyange Division on the city's north-east side. The Bank's documents give no coordinates for Galatiya or for the villages named in the resettlement plan.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49880 (IDA Credit No. 4988-UG) for the Uganda Electricity Sector Development Project (P119737). US$120 million approved 30 June 2011, effective 23 October 2012, revised to US$76.04 million, US$60.56 million disbursed, against a borrower contribution of US$33.2 million of which US$18.6 million was spent. Closing was extended from 28 February 2017 to 31 January 2019. Funds were cancelled at a third restructuring on 18 July 2018. Outcome was rated Moderately Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 February 2021).

cases.conditions: A resettlement action plan for the 137 km line was disclosed in Uganda on 13 December 2010. The Bank's resettlement policy required compensation before any civil works began. The government set up an escrow account to fund compensation payments. The implementing agency was the Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL).

companies.name: Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL)
companies.role: State transmission company; implementing agency for the line and for the resettlement plan
companies.desc: Uganda's state-owned electricity transmission company, which owns and operates the high-voltage grid and acts as single buyer of bulk power.

cases.community: The project's resettlement plan, reviewed and updated in June 2011, says that 'In general, there are 2136 households, and a total of about 13596 persons affected by the currently optimized route in the project area', of whom 160 households were to be physically displaced and had chosen to have their houses replaced, 50 of those able to move onto unencumbered land of their own and 110 described as 'oustees who will need resettlement', while 65 more households with structures to be demolished chose cash. It listed 321 permanent and 121 semi-permanent structures affected and about 225 structures, mainly homes and shops, to be demolished, and named Nabusanke Town A, Kayabwe, Buwama B, Lutente, Lukuli, Kayirikiti, Kalagala Kiteredde, Kamungomba and Namansenene among the places where most of the people to be physically displaced lived, along with the urban centres of Buwama, Lukaaya and Masaka Town Council. The Bank's completion report says the line as built affected 2,661 households against the estimate of 2,136, and that 13,642 resettlement packages were prepared; the report's own results table gives a revised target of 14,452 packages and 11,197 provided at completion. It records a case at Galatiya where the local Anglican church, which UETCL had paid for the right of way in 2012, later sold its land including that right of way to squatters on it, after UETCL delayed registering the title. The new landowners asked UETCL for compensation. Between May 2017 and February 2018 the Bank received three written complaints from one affected person on behalf of the squatters that UETCL had gone ahead with construction without compensating them, and 'UETCL acquired an interim court order and with the aid of armed policemen forcefully carried out works in the disputed area, which contravened OP/BP 4.12'. After a joint Bank mission of 16 to 18 April 2018 the Bank wrote to the client on 30 April asking UETCL not to enforce the order, to show it had lawfully acquired the land, not to evict the title holders and not to settle on terms that would see works completed before compensation; 'UETCL went ahead and carried out the stringing works in contravention of the World Bank safeguards policy, and the landowners commenced legal proceedings against UETCL.' Residents of Nyendo-Ssenyange Division in Masaka told the Daily Monitor in 2015 that they would not move until they were adequately compensated for their property and land and that a promised disturbance allowance had never come; one resident said UETCL had mapped the area in 2008 and told 26 people to stop activities while they waited for compensation, and that the money had not been processed since. UETCL's compensation officer told the paper the project never provided for disturbance allowances.
cases.ecosystem: The line passed through the fringes of seven central forest reserves and one local forest reserve, affecting 32.07 hectares in the corridor. As an offset, 210 hectares were restored in the degraded Gangu central forest reserve in Mpigi and Butambala districts and 10 hectares in Nabijoka local forest reserve in Kalungu district. The Bank also records that the project did not comply with Uganda's wetlands regulations because the conditions on its licence, including culverts to let water flow through wetlands, had not been met.
cases.suppression: UETCL used an interim court order and armed police to carry out works in the disputed area at Galatiya while the occupants were unpaid, which the Bank's completion report says contravened its involuntary resettlement policy.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 13,596 for this project. That figure appears word for word in the project's own 2011 resettlement plan, which says 'In general, there are 2136 households, and a total of about 13596 persons affected by the currently optimized route in the project area', and which repeats it in a summary table as the total number of project-affected persons. It is a count of people affected, not relocated: the same plan sets 160 of those households for physical displacement. The Bank's completion report says the line as built affected 2,661 households, that 13,642 resettlement packages were prepared against a revised target of 14,452 with 11,197 provided at completion, and records that the line was de-energized on 23 July 2018 'to allow for safe relocation of all households living within the line's ROW corridor', without giving a number for how many were moved. No figure is entered here because no document found counts anyone relocated.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says that because of unresolved disputes with landowners and delays in transferring land titles, 'construction works continued along the transmission line, which contravened OP/BP 4.12', and that the slow resolution of the disputes led to conflicts, some reported directly to the Bank. UETCL energized the line on 1 June 2018 without informing the Bank 'and without considering the PAPs and business operators who were still under the line'; the Bank intervened and the line was de-energized on 23 July 2018 to allow households inside the corridor to be moved and the health, safety and environmental issues dealt with, and was re-energized on 19 December 2018. The report says the resettlement plan's implementation was also marred by governance issues that led to the dismissal of the project safeguards officer, and that the only compliance issue still open was the outstanding payments. By project closure on 31 January 2019, 89 per cent of affected people had been compensated, and 93 per cent by December 2020; its table for November 2020 shows 2,464 of 2,661 paid and 197 payments outstanding, held up by deceased claimants without letters of administration, ownership and title disputes, pending title searches and outstanding disclosures. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2021 records the same events and lists lengthy delays in processing payment claims among the problems.

cases.title: Upper Cisokan pumped storage: 765 households moved, a decade of unfinished payments
cases.place: Upper Cisokan reservoirs, access road and quarry, Cipongkor and Rongga districts, West Bandung Regency, West Java, Indonesia
cases.point: Cipongkor district, West Bandung Regency (OpenStreetMap), where the project's quarry and part of its access road sit. The reservoirs also reach Rongga district and the Cibeber and Bojongpicung districts of Cianjur Regency.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-80570 for the Upper Cisokan Pumped Storage Hydro-Electrical Power (1040 MW) Project (P112158), later renamed the Pumped Storage Technical Assistance Project. US$640 million approved 26 May 2011, effective 1 May 2012, revised to US$36.09 million after the project was restructured on 21 December 2018, with US$36.09 million disbursed. Closing was extended from 31 December 2018 to 31 December 2021. The borrower's share was US$160 million at approval and US$77.91 million spent. Total project cost fell from US$800 million to US$114 million (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 June 2022).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD), successor loan
lenders.role: The Bank re-engaged with the scheme through the Development of Pumped Storage Hydropower in Java Bali System Project (P172256, approved 10 September 2021). The Bank's completion report says it was agreed that an action plan on the outstanding land acquisition and resettlement issues, acceptable to the Bank, be fulfilled before that new loan disburses for Upper Cisokan.

cases.conditions: The loan agreement said the borrower must ensure that component 2 of the project, land acquisition, resettlement and rehabilitation, 'is financed exclusively out of its own or other resources and not out' of the Bank loan. The state utility PLN undertook to finance US$160 million for that component, including US$74.4 million of land acquisition. Three land acquisition and resettlement action plans were prepared under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, for the upper and lower reservoirs, for the access road and quarry, and for the transmission lines; the Bank cleared them in 2011 and kept monitoring them after the 2018 restructuring. The Bank's own completion report notes that the US$74.4 million estimate for land acquisition and compensation was not included in a cost figure it gives elsewhere.

companies.name: PT PLN (Perusahaan Listrik Negara)
companies.role: State electricity utility; borrower's implementing agency, which financed and carried out the land acquisition and resettlement
companies.desc: Indonesia's state-owned electricity company, which generates, transmits and distributes most of the country's power.

cases.community: The Bank's completion report says in a footnote that 'the number of households affected by land acquisition was 2,063, including 765 households who were physically resettled'. It says delays in land acquisition and resettlement were flagged as a key risk at the start and that the risk materialised: 'it took a full decade for the acquisition and resettlement to be substantially completed', including compensation payments and livelihood assistance. A review of the resettlement plans that the Bank approved in May 2021 found outstanding items: all remaining land compensation payments to be delivered, compensation for restricting land use inside the transmission line right of way to be delivered, infrastructure support for eligible communities, and 'complete relocation of remaining households in the Upper and Lower Cisokan Reservoirs'. A separate count in the same report says that as of February 2021 the project had acquired 721.92 hectares, 98.65 per cent of the total. The project's land acquisition plan for the access road and quarry names Karangsari village in Cipongkor district as the quarry site and runs the access road through Cijambu, Sarinagen, Sirnagalih, Sukaresmi and Cibitung villages in Cipongkor and Rongga districts. Republika reported on 18 November 2015 that a lawyer for residents, Roedy Wiranatakusumah, accused PLN of building an access road on a 5,130 square metre plot in Sukaresmi village, Rongga district, while a court case over it was still running. The plot's freehold certificate holder, Sulton, had lost at the Bandung administrative court and the case had gone to appeal; the lawyer said Sulton never sold the land to PLN and that an appeal ruling of 5 November 2015 went in Sulton's favour, which the article does not independently confirm. iNews reported on 21 June 2025 that at least 24 houses in Karangsari village, Cipongkor, had cracked walls from rock blasting and crushing at PLN's Gunung Karang andesite quarry for the scheme, that residents of neighbouring Sarinagen also protested, that PLN had offered a one-off payment of 200,000 rupiah which residents had not accepted, and that a West Bandung council commission chairman, Pither Tjuandys, called the amount far too small for a state company. PLN's regional manager, Nugroho Budi Sulaksono, told the paper the houses would be repaired within a week at the latest, that nearly all the damage was minor, and that neither PLN nor the local health office had received reports of residents falling ill from the dust.
cases.displaced_label: households physically resettled (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8,213 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 2,063 households affected by land acquisition, of which 765 households were physically resettled, and says relocation of the remaining households in the two reservoir areas was still outstanding when the Bank reviewed the plans in May 2021. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank's loan was cut from US$640 million to US$36.09 million and the project was renamed a technical assistance project in December 2018; the dam itself was not built under this loan. Compensation payment for household resettlement was recorded as completed in July 2019, eight years after the loan was approved and after the original closing date. The Bank's own review of the resettlement plans in May 2021 still listed outstanding land compensation payments, outstanding payment for restrictions inside the transmission line corridor and the relocation of households still living in the reservoir areas, and made an acceptable action plan on these a condition of disbursement under the successor loan. PLN's own completion review of the plans, finished in 2021, identified outstanding tasks and new issues that had emerged.

cases.title: Kenya's informal settlements upgrading project: six deaths the Bank was not told about
cases.place: Majengo Talai in Kericho and Kwa Hakatsa and Mwatate in Mombasa, among KISIP settlements in 14 Kenyan counties
cases.point: Kericho town (OpenStreetMap), where one of the three settlements needing relocation to other land lies. The project worked in settlements across 14 counties and the Bank's documents give no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-48730 and trust fund TF-18327 for the Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project (P113542). US$100 million of IDA approved 24 March 2011, effective 30 June 2011, with US$99.99 million disbursed by the revised figures and US$93.29 million actually disbursed; the trust fund added US$8.3 million. Closing was extended twice, from 30 June 2016 to 31 May 2018 and then to 30 November 2019. Outcome was rated Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 14 August 2020).

lenders.role: US$45 million at appraisal, revised to US$39 million, with US$38.95 million disbursed (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered three policies: environmental assessment, cultural property and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed on 26 November 2010 and re-disclosed after the mid-term review. Settlement-level resettlement action plans were required where planning, surveying or infrastructure work displaced people; about 70 were needed for the tenure component. The Bank also required that land titles not be released until land for the affected people had been identified and surveyed.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the infrastructure component had about 30,000 project-affected persons, roughly 2 per cent of its beneficiaries, and the tenure component about 18,000, roughly 14 per cent. It says all displacement was in-situ, inside the settlement, 'except for three settlements in Kericho and Mombasa (Kwa Hakatsa, Mwatate and Majengo Talai) where alternative land was required to resettle 82 households (328 PAPs) as they were living on environmentally fragile areas and could not be settled in-situ'. At project closing that move had not happened: land had been identified in Mombasa and the planning and resettlement process had begun, and two options for land were still being explored in Kericho. Of about 70 resettlement plans needed where tenure work caused displacement, about 61 had been cleared and about 40 had been implemented or nearly implemented when the completion report was written; no document found counts the people moved under them. The grievance system handled complaints at settlement, county and national level. Separately, the report records deaths on the project's works. Writing of 'the five fatality cases that were related to KISIP, which took place in 2015 and 2018', it says the issue was first identified from a review of a monthly progress report and that during an October 2018 mission, after the Bank asked the client to confirm all incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, 'the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred'. It says that although there was awareness at local level to report severe injuries and deaths to resident engineers, contractors and the police, 'there was a systemic failure of reporting to KISIP high level management and to the World Bank'.
cases.ecosystem: At project closing many of the drainage networks the project built were clogged with solid waste and wastewater, because residents and counties had not worked out how to collect waste and maintain the upgraded infrastructure.
cases.killed_note: Six deaths in incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, in 2015 and 2018, recorded in the World Bank's completion report. The same paragraph refers to 'the five fatality cases that were related to KISIP' and then says the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred; it accounts for six cases, of which one was treated as resolved, three were in court, one was with an insurance company and one was still in discussion with the contractor. The Bank says the project team committed to enforcing the contracts until the affected families were compensated, with a deadline of the end of August 2020.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 7,952 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives about 30,000 project-affected persons under the infrastructure component and about 18,000 under the tenure component, says all displacement was in-situ apart from 82 households (328 people) in three settlements who needed other land, and records that their resettlement had not been completed when the project closed. No document found counts anyone actually relocated, so no figure is entered here. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome satisfactory. At closing five of the six death cases were unresolved and the Bank said its supervision would continue until they were, and that the resettlement of the 82 households and the remaining resettlement plans, expected to be finished in September 2020, would also be supervised past closing. An action plan including a protocol for reporting incidents was put in place after the deaths came to light.

cases.title: Lower Nzoia irrigation: 568 people unpaid at closing and two drownings
cases.place: Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme and flood dykes, Busia and Siaya counties, Kenya
cases.point: Budalang'i, Bunyala, Busia County (OpenStreetMap), inside the scheme's flood protection and irrigation area. The project also covered Siaya County and a water distribution network in Mombasa.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-52680 (US$155 million), IDA-56740 (US$58 million) and IDA-74230 (US$30 million) and trust fund TF-A0761 (US$3.5 million) for the Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635). Approved 18 June 2013, effective 24 October 2013, closed 31 May 2025. Bank financing of US$243 million was revised down to US$141.24 million with US$147.32 million disbursed. Credits were partly cancelled at restructurings on 4 September 2017 and 25 June 2019 and the closing date was extended four times (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 December 2025).

lenders.name: KfW (Germany)
lenders.role: US$20.01 million in the original financing plan, revised to nil, with US$14,985 recorded as disbursed (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement and environmental assessment policies, along with pest management and physical cultural resources. Four resettlement action plans were prepared by the borrower and cleared by the Bank, for the Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme, the flood infrastructure and the Mombasa water distribution network. The project was restructured to allow land compensation to be paid from IDA funds through a special-purpose account separate from the government's pooled land compensation account, which meant a National Land Commission bank account had to be opened for the purpose.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says that at project closure, 'of the 4,704 PAPs, 88 percent were compensated, while the remaining were 568 PAPs (12 percent) with a value of around US$883,000', and attributes the shortfall to absentee claimants, succession grants, pending affidavits and missing title documents. It says the borrower remains liable and that the National Land Commission must secure and ringfence the money until the unpayable claimants become eligible. It also records 156 grievances about compensation, safeguards, construction and access, of which 142 were resolved; of the 14 left, 11 were about pending compensation. The report says the processes for preparing and clearing the four resettlement plans and for paying compensation took a considerable time and were flagged as contributing to delays across the project. The Star reported on 8 November 2022 that residents of Ugunja, Alego Usonga and Ugenya sub-counties in Siaya and Budalang'i in Busia accepted the project but objected to the 7-metre-wide tertiary canals, which would leave smallholders with little or no land, feared the government would not pay for the land taken for them, and wanted to know where they would be relocated; it says compensation for the main and secondary canals had largely been settled from Ugunja to Block 7 in Usonga ward while the tertiary canals remained unresolved, and that the National Land Commission's compensation gazette notice was dated 21 June 2021.
cases.killed_note: Two deaths by drowning during the project's construction period, recorded in the World Bank's completion report, which says all construction work was immediately suspended, an investigation into the causes was carried out and corrective actions were taken. Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group's review says who drowned or where.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 9,079 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 4,704 project-affected persons, of whom 88 per cent were compensated and 568 were not, with no breakdown between people who lost land and people who lost homes and no count of anyone relocated. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the same figures. No figure is entered here because no document found counts anyone relocated. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank's two documents on this project say different things about its resettlement performance, and both are given here. The completion report says the project complied with the resettlement policy OP 4.12 and that the social safeguards rating 'mostly remained Moderately Satisfactory' including at closing. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the same report says 'the rating for Involuntary Resettlement was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory (MU) by 2018 and remained MU until 2022 when it was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory', with the other social safeguard policies staying moderately satisfactory. At closing 568 claimants worth about US$883,000 were still unpaid, and the Bank said it would monitor the post-closure safeguard action plan twice a year, including through the follow-on project. Of the irrigation works, supporting structures for a second phase were built, and the completion report records that land compensation and related social and environmental problems delayed handing sites to the contractor.

cases.title: Ethiopia's third road sector loan: deaths on the road contracts and no count of the people displaced
cases.place: Gondar-Debark, Aposto-Irba Moda-Negele and Gedo-Nekempte roads, Ethiopia
cases.point: Gondar (OpenStreetMap), at one end of the Gondar-Debark road, one of the three roads built. The Bank's documents do not say where the deaths happened.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-43150 and trust fund TF-56516 for the Road Sector Development Stage III Project (APL3), an adaptable programme loan (P091077). SDR 148.7 million, equivalent to US$225 million, approved 31 May 2007, effective 21 August 2007, mid-term review 21 November 2011, closed 30 June 2015. SDR 148.35 million was disbursed, which the Independent Evaluation Group puts at US$228.17 million against a total project cost of US$386.68 million at appraisal and US$412.6 million actual. The implementing agency was the Ethiopian Roads Authority. At the project's only restructuring, on 23 September 2013, the component for institutional strengthening of the roads authority was dropped and the Yalo-Nehile road was excluded (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 December 2015).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A, full assessment, and triggered the environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement policies. Environmental impact assessments and resettlement action plans were prepared for each of the project roads, together with a resettlement and rehabilitation policy framework. Contractors were bound by environmental monitoring plans, with internal monitoring by the roads authority's environmental monitoring and safety branch and external monitoring by regional and national environmental authorities.
cases.community: The loan paid for six civil works contracts on three roads, covering 499.36 km: the Gondar-Debark trunk road, three contracts on the 268 km Aposto-Irba Moda-Negele link road and two on the 134 km Gedo-Nekempte section of the Addis-Nekempte road. A fourth road, the 70 km Yalo-Nehile gravel road, was in the original design but was dropped at the 2013 restructuring after design errors raised its cost, and was not built under this credit. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the number of project-affected persons was estimated at appraisal at 3,477 households and 19,877 persons, and that 'the cost was estimated are US$285.5 million'; it does not say what that cost covers. It says 'the ICR does not provide any information on the actual number of persons affected by the project' and 'there is no evidence in the ICR that this category A project complied with the involuntary safeguard requirements'. The Bank's completion report says its own finding is that 'the overall performance of the project on safeguards aspects was very weak with relatively very few gains achieved for enhancing the management of social and environmental concerns', that early supervision reports describe deplorable working conditions, in at least one case brought to the attention of local authorities and perhaps the cause of worker strikes, and that one aide memoire of May 2010 records workers paid 10 birr a day against a going rate of 25 birr. It says there is room for improvement in carrying out land acquisition, resettlement and compensation. It says the roads authority's capacity on safeguards was weak, that the regions and districts that actually carry out land acquisition and expropriation 'have little knowledge or awareness of the project's safeguards instruments', and that the roads authority's right-of-way team is not resourced to monitor the resettlement plans. The last outstanding items on one contract included 'resolution of the outstanding ROW compensation issues for the extended contract period'.
cases.ecosystem: The Bank's completion report records deficiencies in environmental mitigation during construction: treatment of cut slopes, reinstatement of quarry sites and borrow pits, disposal of spoil material and handling of bitumen and oils.
cases.killed_note: Footnote 10 of the World Bank's completion report says 'over 30 deaths were reported in several incidents due road crashes and improper safety procedures with use of heavy equipment'. The footnote hangs on a passage saying that health and safety concerns led to 'the unnecessary and preventable loss of lives and properties in the project contracts, lives of workers as well as road users and community residents due to accidents'. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the figure and attributes the deaths to contractors not complying with basic road safety requirements and to the roads authority not having the staff to supervise them. The deaths are not counted in the figure above: 'over 30' is a floor and not a count, the deaths were spread over several incidents across six civil works contracts on three roads, and neither document says which contract or place any of them happened on.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 15,015 for this project. The Bank's appraisal estimate, as recorded by the Independent Evaluation Group, was 3,477 households and 19,877 persons affected. The Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives no information on the actual number of people affected, and no document found counts anyone relocated. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at. No displacement figure is given here because none of the Bank's documents records an outcome.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report rated safeguards performance very weak and said health and safety concerns led to 'the unnecessary and preventable loss of lives and properties in the project contracts'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 November 2016 says there is no explicit statement in the completion report about compliance with environmental safeguards and no evidence that this category A project complied with the involuntary resettlement requirements. The Bank says the roads authority's commitment and capacity improved in later years, across its whole portfolio and not only on Bank-financed projects.

Neither document names the places where the deaths happened, gives an exact number, or counts anyone relocated, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives no information on the actual number of people affected. This project is one of a series: separate cases on this map cover the fourth phase of the same programme on the Mekenajo-Dembidolo road and the Mizan-Dima road under a later Ethiopian transport credit. Those are different corridors and different loans.

cases.title: Uganda's rural electrification credit: lines built before the people under them were paid
cases.place: Rural grid extension lines across Uganda, with a focus on the north; point at Kampala

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-45540 and IDA-52340 for the Energy for Rural Transformation Project APL-2 (P112334), a credit of SDR 57.6 million (US$87 million equivalent). Approved 6 April 2009, effective 25 November 2009, closing extended from 30 June 2013 to 30 June 2016, with restructurings on 23 May 2014 and 13 February 2015. Original commitment SDR 49.50 million plus SDR 8.10 million, against SDR 54.51 million disbursed. The project was environmental category B. The implementing agencies included the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development and the Rural Electrification Agency. The outcome was rated Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 June 2017).

lenders.role: Grant TF-10096 of US$5.5 million, of which US$5.49 million was disbursed (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy because its works took land or limited access to land, along with policies on forests, dam safety and international waterways. A resettlement policy framework and an environmental and social management framework were prepared at appraisal. The resettlement policy required that compensation be paid in full before any civil works began. A government directive required that compensation be paid only through formal bank accounts.
cases.community: The project extended the rural electricity grid, building 12 distribution lines of almost 1,300 km, and took land and wayleaves for them. The Bank's completion report says the overall safeguards rating 'remained Satisfactory until May 2014 when the rating was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory due to delayed payment of compensations to Project Affected Persons (PAPs) even after most of the grid extension lines and expansion projects had been completed. This was non-compliant with World Bank OP 4.12, which required complete compensations to PAPs prior to the commencement of any civil works.' It says the delays were put down to the directive requiring payment through bank accounts, which most affected people in rural areas did not have. On three further grid extension lines financed at the February 2015 restructuring, it says, 'construction works had finalized well before compensation to PAPs was completed'. The resettlement plan's closure report records that cash payments were finished in December 2016, six months after the project closed, with nearly 90 per cent of affected people paid, rising to over 96 per cent by 1 June 2017, and that an escrow account was opened to hold the money for those still unpaid. The report also records recurring differences between the people identified in the resettlement plans and those identified in the detailed engineering designs, which it says caused contention and conflict among affected people and local leaders. The Bank's own account of its borrower's performance says 'the GoU violated the World Bank OP 4.12 when commenced and even finalized construction of grid extension lines before completing compensation payments to PAPs', and that the money for those payments was not transferred to the Rural Electrification Agency in time. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 14 November 2017 says the agency 'was in noncompliance with the Bank's policy by allowing the start of the construction works before the completion of compensation payments' and that, while the government was late releasing the funds, the agency was also slow to pay when funds were available. No document found gives the number of people affected, counts anyone relocated or names a line or a community.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 12,239 for this project. No Bank document found gives any count of people affected, compensated or relocated, so no figure is entered here. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Satisfactory and its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group records that weak Bank supervision on the resettlement policy resulted in non-compliance. Compensation payments were still being made a year after the project closed. The Independent Evaluation Group also records that some staff of the Rural Electrification Agency were found to have been involved in fraud and corruption over the verification of solar equipment installations.

extend.why: Lead 8 is the same loan as this case: the Uganda Transport Sector Development Project, P092837, whose cancellation the card already records. The existing card covers the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road and rests on the Inspection Panel's investigation. The project's own completion report adds firmer loan figures, its own compensation figures for that road, the Bank's verdict on the safeguards category, and compensation shortfalls on two other corridors paid for by the same credits. Those two corridors are a different place and are added as a fact about the credits, not as part of this episode.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), full credit detail
lenders_add.role: Credit IDA-46790, SDR 120 million (US$190 million equivalent), approved 10 December 2009 and effective 15 July 2010; additional credit IDA-49490, SDR 47.4 million (US$75 million equivalent), approved by the Board in 2010 and signed later; and grant TF-11094 of GBP 6.05 million (US$8.0 million equivalent) from the United Kingdom's Department for International Development, for the Transport Sector Development Project (P092837). The revised commitment was SDR 106.96 million. The Bank suspended disbursements on 22 October 2015 for the borrower's failure to implement the project in line with environmental and social standards, and cancelled the project on 21 December 2015 with the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road 49 per cent complete; the government continued the road with its own funds. The outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance were all rated Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 5 June 2017).

add.community_add: The completion report gives its own compensation figures for this road: 2,246 of 2,844 identified people had been compensated, 79 per cent, rising to 94 per cent by 27 March 2017. It says the original estimate of 2,430 people was based on sampling rather than a full census, and that a later sweep by surveyors and valuation experts added another 414 people eligible for compensation. These are a different count from the Inspection Panel's 2,455 people owed resettlement pay with 209 claims still outstanding in mid-2016; the two sources count at different dates and neither document reconciles them. The report says the significant social concerns the communities raised, including sexual violence against children by road workers, increased child labour and school dropouts, more accidents on the road and at the stone quarry, a rise in crime, poor compensation practices and an unclear redress mechanism, 'were not responded to adequately in a timely manner'. The same credits also paid for two roads in northern Uganda, which are not part of this episode, and the completion report gives compensation shortfalls on both. On the Gulu-Atiak road, 1,884 of 2,027 affected people were compensated, 93 per cent, with ten of the unpaid claims in court and the rest awaiting reassessment. On the Vurra-Oraba road, 3,276 of 3,935 were compensated, 83 per cent; the report says the shortfall arose because extra affected people were identified after compensation was supposed to have been concluded and no money had been budgeted for land acquisition that year, and records in a footnote 'over 200 complaints of non-payment due to bounced payments and missing documentation'.
add.conditions_add: The 2011 environmental and social impact assessment for the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road proposed category A; during preparation of the additional financing this was downgraded to category B. The Bank's completion report says that given the complex and systemic social issues that emerged during implementation and the fact that the road runs through a national park, 'this change in the safeguard category was an error of judgment'. A 13.3 km section of the road crosses Kibale National Park, where the design had originally kept the road unwidened to avoid taking land and destroying tree canopies, partly to reduce road kills of primates crossing at road level. On 22 December 2014 the Uganda Wildlife Authority approved the wider cross-section through the park, an option the impact assessment had rejected, on condition that only a limited number of trees be removed and additional speed humps installed.
add.displaced_note_add: ICIJ gives 12,882 for this project. The Bank's completion report counts people identified for compensation rather than people relocated: 2,027 on Gulu-Atiak, 3,935 on Vurra-Oraba and 2,844 on Kamwenge-Fort Portal. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), Integrated Growth Poles Project
lenders_add.role: The Integrated Growth Poles Project (P083351) was approved on 12 July 2005, became effective on 28 September 2005 and closed on 31 December 2014 against an original closing date of 31 December 2010. It was financed by credits IDA-41010 and IDA-43990, with an original commitment of SDR 85.90 million revised to SDR 107.56 million and SDR 107.31 million disbursed; the additional credit of SDR 25 million (US$40 million) was approved by the Bank's board in April 2008 and the financing agreement signed on 8 May 2008. The project covered Antananarivo-Antsirabe, Nosy Be and Taolagnaro (Fort Dauphin). Its Fort Dauphin component built a new public port on the Ehoala peninsula under a public-private partnership with Rio Tinto and part-rehabilitated the existing port. The Bank's completion report lists, among the component's safeguards activities, 'implementation of RAPs for the QMM's mining facility and Ehoala Port' and water supply and sanitation schemes for project-affected people. Because the Bank financed Ehoala Port as an associated investment supporting Rio Tinto's mining, Rio Tinto also had to comply with Bank safeguard policies. The project was environmental category A and an independent expert advisory panel monitored safeguards compliance during preparation and implementation (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 15 June 2015).

add.community_add: The Bank's completion report says QMM's mining investment 'also created significant safeguards challenges in the mining communes', that the income and livelihood restoration programme QMM ran for residents of the mining communes 'was marked by recurring disputes over the prices the company paid to buy their land and the employment policy at its mining facility', and that this prompted local residents at various times to roadblock QMM construction sites and facilities, 'with the most recent flare up in early 2013 when they blocked the mine compound entrance, trapping more than 200 staff inside'. It says the grievance mechanisms the Bank set up during the project and QMM's social programmes helped manage the disputes and prevent violent escalation, but that 'some tensions linger' among residents 'who still feel they were unfairly compensated'. A footnote records that an independent audit of the project's resettlement action plan was launched in 2014 to examine compliance with paragraph 24 of OP 4.12 and paragraph 16 of BP 4.12, and refers to 'PAPs that have yet to obtain compensation at agreed levels following the RAP Audit'. A table in the report's annex, sourced to Rio Tinto's own 2009 information report, lists 'support to the populations affected by the resettlement scheme' through monetary compensation, restitution in kind, house rehabilitation and support measures, naming the resettled population, affected people at Ilafitsinana and villagers from Lohalovoka and Ambinanibe; the same table lists compensation to fishermen and to the people of Ambinanibe, Lohalovoka and Ilafitsinana. The report also records an acute bout of consumer price inflation during construction of the mine and the port, declining employment after the construction period, and an increased risk of HIV/AIDS.
add.displaced_note_add: ICIJ gives 8,911 displaced for Madagascar's Integrated Growth Poles project, drawn from World Bank documents and current to 31 December 2014. The Bank's completion report for that project names the resettlement plans and the villages involved but gives no count of households or people relocated, and the figures in its annex come from Rio Tinto's own report rather than from the Bank. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.

extend.why: Lead 20, the Ethiopia Irrigation and Drainage Project (P092353), is the same episode as this existing case: the same credit, the same two irrigation schemes and the Ribb dam, the same years and the same completion report. It was drafted as a new case and is instead an extend. It adds the credit numbers, the Bank's finding that the project was out of compliance with OP 4.12, and the first independent field study found on this resettlement, which gives the number of households actually relocated and where they went. It also corrects the card's displacement figure, which at present is ICIJ's estimate.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), full credit detail
lenders_add.role: Credits IDA-43330 and IDA-49760 for the Ethiopia Irrigation and Drainage Project, also called the Ethiopian Nile Irrigation and Drainage Project (P092353). US$100 million approved 21 June 2007, effective 24 January 2008, with US$60 million of additional financing approved 23 June 2011 (P125307). The original total of US$160 million was revised to US$121.3 million and US$105.8 million was disbursed. Closing was extended from 31 October 2015 to 31 October 2017. The project was environmental category A and the implementing agency was the Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Electricity. Bank performance was rated Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 10 January 2019).

add.conditions_add: Seven resettlement action plans were approved by the Bank, three for Megech-Seraba, one for Ribb and three for the Ribb dam, with compensation and livelihood restoration costed at US$21.7 million, of which the government funded US$11.17 million. The Bank's policy required compensation before works began. At the final restructuring in October 2017 the financing plan was changed so that credit money could pay US$9.68 million in cash compensation to 6,618 affected people and livelihood restoration payments to 1,486 of them, after the credit had closed.
add.community_add: A 2020 master's thesis at Addis Ababa University by Teketel Adefres is the first independent field study found on this resettlement. Citing the Ethiopian Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Energy's livelihood relocation report of May 2018, it gives 1,486 households on the final net list of affected households, of whom 227 lost all their farmland and housing and were relocated to the towns of Ebinat and Debre Tabor, 38 households to Ebinat and 189 to Debre Tabor, where they were given urban plots for houses and working areas for licensed groups. The affected kebeles it names, from the same ministry report, are Medeb Gubda, Jara Shekera and Ayva Niva in Farta woreda and Ziha and Amisteya in Ibinat woreda. Adefres surveyed 115 of those 227 relocated households with a questionnaire. Of the 115 who answered, he reports that 6.96 per cent had access to all of the basic services he measured together, which he lists as clean energy, clean water supply, sanitation, road access, school, finance, market access and due compensation; that 8.7 per cent had received income-generating activities; and that 33.0 per cent had market access. He concludes that almost all of the resettled households are leading unsustainable livelihoods and that women are excluded from livelihood opportunities. These are his own survey findings, from one master's thesis, not an established record.
add.outcome_add: The Bank's completion report says social safeguards performance was unsatisfactory 'primarily due to protracted delays in making compensation payments and supporting livelihood restoration for the PAPs in the Ribb reservoir and dam construction site', that the delays caused 'increasing frustration on the part of the affected communities and rising tension in the project areas', and that 'throughout much of the project implementation period, the project was not in compliance with OP 4.12 and posed high social risk. It was only after credit closure that the project could be brought into compliance through the use of the Credit to cover the costs.' Of the 4,000 hectares targeted at Megech-Seraba only 1,000 hectares were ready for use, the Bank's economic analysis at closing found the project not economically viable, and Bank management refused a further extension.
add.displaced_label_set: households that lost all farmland and housing and were relocated to Ebinat and Debre Tabor towns (Ethiopian Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Energy relocation report of 2018, as given in Adefres, 2020)
add.displaced_note_set: The card's present figure of 10,409 is ICIJ's estimate and is not a count of people moved; it should be replaced. ICIJ gives 10,409 for this project, drawn from World Bank documents and current to 31 December 2014. The World Bank's completion report gives 6,618 project-affected persons identified and unpaid at the end of the project, covering both temporary loss of access to land during redistribution and construction and permanent relocation because of the Ribb dam and reservoir, and a table listing 226 eligible people at the Ribb dam and reservoir, 3,210 at Megech-Seraba and 3,180 at Ribb irrigation. A 2020 Addis Ababa University master's thesis, citing the Ethiopian ministry's 2018 relocation report, gives 1,486 affected households of whom 227 were relocated. The Bank's 1,486 is given as persons and the ministry's as households. The documents do not explain these differences and no document found reconciles them with ICIJ's figure.
add.confidence_note_add: The unpaid compensation, the breach of the Bank's own resettlement policy and the tension in the project areas are stated in the World Bank's own completion report and repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which are the lender reporting on its own project. The count of 227 relocated households, the towns they were moved to and the living conditions afterwards come from one independent source, a 2020 Addis Ababa University master's thesis, which cites an Ethiopian ministry relocation report of 2018 for the counts and reports its own survey of 115 of the 227 households for the conditions.

sources_add.title: Effects of Resettlement Schemes on the Livelihood of Project Affected Households: The Case of Ribb Irrigation Dam, Amhara Regional State, Ethiopia (master's thesis, College of Development Studies)

dropped.candidate: ET-Road Sector Proj (APL2) to support Govt's RSDP (P082998)
dropped.reason: No document counts anyone relocated and no document records a specific harm to identifiable people, so the case fails both limbs of this round's rule. Opened the World Bank's completion report of 12 December 2012 (ICR2386, 56 pages, read in full from disk) and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 9 December 2013 (read in full). The completion report uses the word resettlement four times, each time in a list of what a construction supervision contract was to cover, and gives no figure for people affected, compensated or moved. Its safeguards section says overall safeguards compliance was rated Satisfactory, that environmental compliance was downgraded to Moderately Satisfactory in October 2009 after issues over workers' health and safety and environmental protection, and that several environmental and social safeguards issues persisted to the end of the project; it gives no deaths, injuries or counts. The Independent Evaluation Group says of the involuntary resettlement policy that 'the ICR only reports that overall safeguards compliance ...was rated Satisfactory. No other details are provided', and repeats that no details are provided. The roads were the Assela-Dodola-Goba and Shashemene-Dodola sections, GobGob-Weldiya, Shire-Adwa-Adiabun, Magna-Mechara and Assosa/Sherkole-Guba, none of which is covered by an existing case on this map. ICIJ gives 12,655 for this project; nothing in the Bank's documents supports or explains it.

dropped.candidate: Ethiopia Urban Local Government Development Project (P101474)
dropped.reason: No document counts anyone relocated, no document records a specific harm to identifiable people, and the Bank judged the project unlikely to displace anyone, so the case fails both limbs of this round's rule. Opened the World Bank's completion report of 8 June 2015 (ICR00003524, 56 pages, read in full from disk) and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 14 October 2015 (read in full). The completion report says the project was classified environmental category B, partial assessment, 'because the planned urban infrastructure and services were not expected to result in environmental damage or significant resettlement', and that an environmental and social management framework and a resettlement policy framework were prepared for subprojects identified during implementation. It says cities' compliance with safeguards requirements was generally satisfactory by the midpoint of the project but that cities 'were less vigilant about ensuring that infrastructure subprojects were constructed and operated in accordance with the recommendations of the EMPs'. The Independent Evaluation Group says the project's safeguards requirements were deemed satisfactory at closure. Neither document gives any count of people affected, compensated or moved. ICIJ gives 9,021 for this project.
